title: A slower flame outlasted the faster flame
question: Which comparison supports a claim about how long SIBAL burned?
record: LUCI burned 5 × 30 cm cotton–fiberglass fabric downward in simulated lunar gravity. Its flame base advanced at 0.9 mm/s versus 1.5 at 1 g, and its tip at 1.1 versus 2.8 mm/s. Fabric extinction occurred about 45 seconds later in the partial-gravity run.
decision: Use the LUCI fabric pair for extinction. Use the aircraft comparison for early spread.
reason: A separate 20-second aircraft test matched the fuel, 5 cm width, direction, approximate gravity and initial atmosphere. It measured base spread of 0.86 mm/s versus 0.92 on LUCI. The centrifuge drop test reported 1.1 mm/s.
limit: The rocket spun, two fuels burned in a shared chamber, and oxygen declined from about 20% to 18% over the fabric observation while the 1-g comparison stayed near 20%. The 45 seconds is an approximate difference for this comparison. It does not give a universal gravity multiplier.
next: Repeat the pair with one material per chamber, matched initial gas and ignition, measured local flow, synchronized oxygen and images, and a fixed definition of extinction. Observe through extinction or record that the run ended first.

options.mechanism: Keep flame-base speed, tip speed and time to extinction for each material and run side by side.
options.tradeoff: Needs aligned definitions and timing for both runs.
options.proof: Return later extinction together with both lower speeds for the LUCI fabric.

options.mechanism: Record when observation starts, when it ends, and whether the flame remained visible at the end.
options.tradeoff: Short experiments often give lower bounds only.
options.proof: A flame still present at the end of a parabola has an unresolved extinction time.

options.name: Experiment matching
options.mechanism: Select comparisons separately for geometry, flow direction and endpoint before ranking conditions.
options.tradeoff: The nearest run changes with the question.
options.proof: Select the aircraft run for early base speed and the LUCI ground comparison for duration.

options.name: Competing explanations
options.mechanism: Record the oxygen history, simultaneous second fuel and centrifugal effects as rival explanations of the difference.
options.tradeoff: The available runs cannot identify their individual contributions.
options.proof: Reject an isolated causal estimate for gravity while retaining the observed direction.

options.name: Image-based reanalysis
options.mechanism: Estimate the width, base and tip independently from timestamped original images with a scale reference.
options.tradeoff: Requires complete video, calibration, a defined visibility threshold and repeat labeling.
options.proof: Two analysts agree within prespecified timing tolerance; otherwise report their disagreement.

options.name: Prospective validation
options.mechanism: Register a matched, single-fuel repeat with an independent run held back from analysis choices.
options.tradeoff: Replicated long-duration partial-gravity tests are scarce.
options.proof: Test a signed prediction against new burns, report sample variation and any censored run.

check: Answer with the material, the approximate paired duration difference and the separate direction of change in speed. Attribute the time comparison to LUCI.

title: Blackened Nomex beside a burning acrylic strip
question: In Saffire-II sample 2-7, which part of the composite ignited?
record: An upstream 5 cm PMMA strip overlapped Nomex HT90-40. At about 22.1% oxygen and 20 cm/s concurrent flow in orbital microgravity, PMMA was consumed. The first centimetre of Nomex was damaged and the first five were blackened. Table I records zero Nomex burn length.
decision: Assign combustion to the PMMA, damage to the Nomex, and no observed Nomex ignition in this test.
reason: The authors distinguish the PMMA flame plume from ignition of the downstream fabric and identify deposited soot as a possible contributor to discoloration.
limit: The 140 s in the table belongs to the composite experiment. Related 1-g tests of externally heated HT90-40 found burning supported by a PMMA flame under some conditions. Changing the grade, pressure, oxygen or external heating changes the scope.
next: Compare flight and ground runs at the component level. For a lunar question, match the flight-grade textile, overlap, oxygen, pressure and heat flux and measure whether flame spread continues after the heat source ends.

options.tradeoff: Requires controlled laboratory data.
options.proof: Report component ignition and post-source spread separately across replicates.

title: After the visible heptane flame disappeared
question: Which FLEX run supports continued combustion after the visible flame went out?
record: In FLEX-155, a free-floating heptane droplet burned in 18% O₂, 67% N₂ and 15% CO₂ at about 1 atm. Its initial/visible-extinction diameters were 2.73/2.52 mm. Subsequent high vaporization, a plateau and cloud formation led the investigators to infer cool-flame burning. In FLEX-120, a vapor cloud also formed, but its ultraviolet instrument recorded no images and the authors found the evidence inconclusive.
decision: Retain an inferred cool-flame phase for FLEX-155 and unresolved cool-flame status for FLEX-120.
reason: The technical report interprets multiple time-resolved observations for each run. A visible endpoint in the experimental table refers to the hot luminous flame.
limit: FLEX-120 used a translated, fiber-supported droplet, 40% CO₂ and about 0.70 atm. The pair cannot isolate the effect of dilution. These are liquid heptane experiments in microgravity.
next: Use synchronized droplet-size, optical and radiometric data with flagging for missing instruments. Compare matched initial diameters, diluent, support and pressure before estimating a suppression threshold.

title: Kapton and Teflon smoke at the alarm threshold
question: Can a detector that responds well to overheated cellulose be assumed to detect smoke from wiring insulation?
record: Meyer et al. compared signals from two detector technologies against alarm thresholds in SAME. The ISS light-scattering detector would have missed over half of the Kapton smoke tests and two-thirds of the Teflon tests. It responded strongly to several larger-particle smokes.
decision: Judge performance by source material, detector type and threshold. Keep this finding separate from time to alarm in an occupied habitat.
reason: Particles from overheated materials have different size distributions. The experiments measured the signal against defined thresholds, with no single response representing every material.
limit: The quoted fractions apply to the published test subsets, with no per-material denominator asserted here. The Shuttle ionization detector had fewer usable data. Dust, transport, filtration and layout matter to an installed detector. The commanded smoke-generation duration in PSI is not time to alarm.
next: Select a sensor comparison with matched fuel, heating, flow and aerosol aging. Measure detection probability alongside nuisance alarms and transport delay under relevant ventilation.

title: Where the 85% oxygen actually went
question: Does an 85% oxygen CFI-G test provide evidence for a solid fabric in an 85% oxygen cabin?
record: CFI-G inverse tests 21202A1 and A2 used an 85% oxygen burner stream flowing into nitrogen with 6% ethane in the chamber. The dissertation tabulates nominal oxygen mass flows of 0.93 and 1.86 mg/s. A1 had no hot ignition. A2 ignited and self-extinguished after 2 seconds.
decision: Use these rows to study a gaseous inverse flame and the role of flow. Exclude their burner oxygen values from cabin-atmosphere and solid-fabric comparisons.
reason: The measurement location changes the physical meaning of the oxygen percentage. The investigators give the feed direction in Methods and tabulate the runs as inverse flames.
limit: The test matrix quotes nominal 2.0 atm. PSI has its own approximate initial pressure readings and unit labels. Use the value from the cited record in its stated units. Two consecutive trials alone cannot isolate a causal oxygen-flow effect.
next: Compare matched normal and inverse configurations with explicit burner and chamber fields. For textile transfer, collect a separate solid-fuel record with measured ambient composition.

title: Opposite directions in five-second material tests
question: Does the same 1-g extrapolation describe P213 tape and polycarbonate at simulated lunar gravity?
record: At 8.2 psia, Urban et al. found the lunar buoyant extinction limit for acrylic-adhesive P213 tape below the WSTF 1-g forced-flow extrapolation. For polycarbonate, the paper reports a lunar extinction oxygen concentration substantially above the WSTF data. Nomex Velcro also showed the latter behavior.
decision: Keep a different conclusion for each material. Preserve the comparator named in each result.
reason: The P213 comparison is explicitly against an extrapolated line. The polycarbonate passage compares against the WSTF data, with a proposed shift onto the quenching branch. Table 2 gives a separate conservative extrapolation for a possible correction.
limit: Both research facilities used a five-second extinction endpoint; NASA Test 1 uses five specimens and burn-length plus debris criteria. Ignition procedures differ between research rigs. The local lunar buoyant velocity was unknown. Table 2 values for P213 and polycarbonate (1.4 and 2.3 oxygen percentage points) describe the authors’ worst-case slope methodology, rather than measured shifts.
next: Reproduce the material-specific comparison with a longer duration, measured local flow and the same matched ignition history. Keep signed observations separate from engineering margins.

title: Four planned lunar burns and an unscored forecast
question: What can the four planned Synergy Pro burns test, and what remains a prediction?
record: Ferkul et al. specify four separate 2 × 20 cm exposed Synergy Pro Navy fabric strips at 8.2 ± 0.3 psia, with initial oxygen of 37%, 33%, 29% and 25%. Their concept gives an expected lunar limiting oxygen concentration of 24–26%. They expect the first three tests to burn to threshold and the fourth not to ignite.
decision: Use the published qualitative expectation as a baseline. Treat the guide’s 26% mean and 1.5 percentage-point spread as an illustrative assumption until an independent timestamped team forecast is supplied.
reason: FM² refreshes the chamber between burns; oxygen can fall during a burn. Initial oxygen, successful ignition, post-igniter spread and oxygen at extinction are different measurements.
limit: The reviewed sources are design and planning documents. No completed lunar outcomes or independently time-stamped team forecast was located. A deterministic limiting-oxygen model describes propagation conditional on establishment; a failed igniter, absent evidence or short observation must not become a scored negative.
next: Predefine each outcome, invalid-test handling, sensor requirements and scoring horizon. Preserve the forecast and its timestamp independently before using public outcome data.
